strengths: Introduces a novel inference-time robust multi-objective alignment framework for LLMs, addressing the practical issue that objective weights are often unknown at deployment.

Provides a clean theoretical formulation as a max-min game between weights and policy, proves existence of Nash equilibrium, reduces the problem to convex optimization, and derives an analytic best-response policy.
The practical blockwise algorithm is computationally efficient, reuses candidate blocks, and is shown to have latency comparable to standard controlled decoding.
Empirical results on Helpful-Harmless, UltraFeedback, and ValuePrism show improved worst-case rewards and win rates, with ablations over λ, block size, and number of objectives.
The KKT analysis gives useful insight into how RMOD equalizes rewards across objectives and how λ controls weight sparsity.
weaknesses: The Monte Carlo approximation in Equation (10) and Algorithm 2 appears technically incorrect: sampling z_k from π_ref and then weighting by π_ref(z_k) does not unbiasedly estimate E_{z~π_ref}[f(z)], so the practical weight update may optimize a biased objective.

There is a substantial gap between the theoretical Algorithm 1 and the practical Algorithm 2: the practical variant replaces best-response sampling with argmax best-of-K block selection and uses approximate weight updates without any Nash-equilibrium or robustness guarantee.

Value functions are trained as reward predictors via CD-FUDGE rather than true value functions, so the theoretical guarantees do not directly apply to the implemented method, and no error bounds or sensitivity analysis are provided.

Evaluation is incomplete on UltraFeedback and ValuePrism: comparisons are mostly limited to UNIFORM and single-objective baselines, with no robust training baselines (e.g., MaxMin-RLHF) or other strong multi-objective inference-time baselines.
The robust objective is optimized greedily per decoding block under the reference continuation policy, which may be myopic and not globally robust over full sequences.
Some claims, such as outperforming baselines by up to 20%, are not fully contextualized, and the advantages over closer robust or worst-case-aware baselines are not convincingly demonstrated.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: multi-objective alignment of LLMs at inference time without requiring predefined objective weights.
Provides a clean maximin game formulation and derives a convex optimization problem for worst-case weights, with a closed-form best-response policy.
Introduces a practical blockwise decoding variant that reduces latency relative to exact token-wise robust decoding.
Evaluates on three multi-objective datasets (HH, UltraFeedback, ValuePrism) and reports consistent improvements over uniform and single-objective baselines in worst-case metrics.
Code is promised to be available, and the appendix supplies derivations, experimental details, and additional analyses.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the maximin objective over the simplex essentially reduces to maximizing the minimum reward; the convex log-sum-exp reformulation and KL-regularized best-response policy are standard, and the paper is incremental relative to prior robust alignment work.

The practical Algorithm 2 is not theoretically justified: it optimizes weights using the same K samples later used for selection, and it replaces sampling from the best-response policy with a greedy argmax over sampled blocks, so the claimed Nash-equilibrium connection no longer holds.

The weight update in Algorithm 2 and Equation (12) lacks an explicit simplex normalization/projection step; as written, the weights may leave the simplex, which undermines the convex optimization and Nash-equilibrium guarantees.

Missing comparisons to relevant robust-alignment baselines such as max-min RLHF, group-robust preference optimization, distributionally robust optimization, or CVaR-style methods, despite citing them as related robust approaches.

Evaluation is incomplete: the paper mainly compares against uniform and single-objective decoding, with only modest worst-case win-rate gains (e.g., around 57% on UltraFeedback), no confidence intervals or significance tests, and no average-reward/Pareto trade-off analysis.

The method uses the same reward models to train value functions and to evaluate generated responses, with no human evaluation or independent validation, creating a risk of reward-model over-optimization.

Theoretical guarantees assume exact value functions and exact expectations over all possible continuations, while the practical algorithm relies on learned value functions and a small sampled candidate set; the impact of these approximations is not analyzed.

The worst-case-over-all-weightings objective is extremely pessimistic and may sacrifice average performance; the paper does not adequately justify when this notion of robustness is preferable to Pareto or average-reward alignment.

Some notational and algorithmic details are unclear or inconsistent, e.g., variable naming in Algorithm 2, missing details about the number of weight-update iterations, and limited reproducibility information for the value-function training.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: multi-objective inference-time alignment when preference weights are unknown or misspecified.
Provides a clean theoretical formulation as a maximin game between reward weights and decoding policy, with existence of Nash equilibrium, minimax interchange, and a closed-form best-response policy.
Reduces the weight optimization to a convex log-sum-exp problem and gives a practical blockwise best-of-K variant with reportedly minimal overhead and latency comparable to controlled decoding.
Evaluation is broad across HH, UltraFeedback, and ValuePrism, with multiple baselines including UNIFORM, single-objective decoding, GRPO/DPO, Rewarded Soups, and MOD.
Includes useful ablations over block size, K, lambda, and number of objectives, plus qualitative examples and an available code release.
Theoretical analysis of optimal weights suggests intuitive worst-case equalization and sparsity behavior controlled by lambda.
weaknesses: The Monte Carlo approximation in Equation (10) and Algorithm 2 appears mathematically inconsistent: sampling z_k ~ pi_ref should approximate E_{z~pi_ref}[f(z)] by (1/K) sum_k f(z_k), but the paper uses sum_k pi_ref(z_k) f(z_k). This estimates E[pi_ref(z)f(z)], not the stated objective, and biases optimization toward high-probability blocks, undermining the claimed solution of Equation (7).

The practical Algorithm 2 does not solve the Nash equilibrium described by the theory: it selects an argmax over sampled blocks rather than sampling from the best-response policy, uses a gradient update, and has no convergence or performance guarantee for the practical variant.

Evaluation depends entirely on automated reward models that are also used to define the optimization objective, creating a serious risk of reward hacking/overoptimization; no human evaluation or held-out reward model validation is provided.

Novelty is incremental: robust/minimax multi-objective alignment has been studied in RLHF, and the paper combines this idea with controlled decoding; the core algorithmic ingredients are largely existing techniques.

The claim of alignment 'without any information about weights' is somewhat overstated, as lambda remains a critical hyperparameter controlling worst-case focus and sparsity, and value functions must still be trained.

Value functions are trained on reference-policy prefixes, but robust decoding shifts the prefix distribution; there is no analysis of value estimation error or robustness under this distribution shift.
Experiments use a relatively small reference model (gemma-2-2b-it) and GPT-2-based value functions, leaving unclear how well the method scales to larger LLMs and more diverse reward models.

Baselines omit several relevant robust or multi-objective RLHF alignment methods, and the comparison relies on reimplemented GRPO-based rewards, which may not fully represent the best available alternatives.

strengths: Formulates robust multi-objective decoding as a novel maximin game between reward weights and the sampling policy, with a clean minimax reduction to a convex optimization over weights and a closed-form best-response policy.

Provides a practical blockwise implementation using value functions and approximate weight updates, with a distilled variant that can reduce inference cost while maintaining strong worst-case performance.
Evaluates across multiple multi-objective alignment datasets (HH, UltraFeedback, ValuePrism), includes ablations over block size, K, and lambda, and reports LLM-as-judge and latency analyses.

The theoretical derivation connecting the minimax objective to log-sum-exp optimization is elegant and supports an efficient implementation with minimal measured overhead compared with controlled decoding baselines.
weaknesses: Novelty and positioning are limited: prior work such as Yoon et al. (2024) already considers group-robust best-of-K decoding at inference time, yet it is not used as a direct baseline and the claim of being first to consider a max-min robust inference-time objective is questionable.

The theoretical objective maximizes the worst-case expected value under a one-step deviation/continuation under the reference policy, not the final worst-case reward used in evaluation; the practical argmax selection also does not exactly sample from the derived best-response policy, weakening the claimed connection between theory and algorithm.

Empirical gains over the most comparable controlled-decoding baseline (UNIFORM) are modest in several key metrics, e.g., LLM-as-judge worst-case win rate 59.1% vs. 57.6%, with no statistical significance tests; claims such as 'up to 20%' improvement are not clearly supported for the main apples-to-apples comparison.

Evaluation has gaps: no direct comparison to prior robust inference-time/best-of-K methods, no systematic validation of value-function accuracy across objectives, and the robust fine-tuning baseline is self-implemented rather than drawn from prior work.

Clarity and reproducibility have issues: the latency table is incomplete/inconsistently formatted, the anonymized code link appears missing, and notation/reference inconsistencies exist (e.g., Proposition/Theorem numbering and the weight update lacking an explicit simplex normalization step).

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: robust multi-objective alignment of LLMs at inference time without requiring users to specify objective weights.

Provides a clean theoretical formulation of the maximin game between objective weights and the decoding policy, with connections to Nash equilibrium, KL-regularized best-response policies, and a convex log-sum-exp weight optimization problem.

Practical blockwise algorithm is reasonably motivated, includes value-function training, approximate weight optimization, and a distilled variant; additional ablations over block size, K, and lambda are provided.

Evaluation spans multiple datasets (Anthropic HH, UltraFeedback, ValuePrism), up to 10 objectives, and several metrics including worst-case reward, worst-case win rate, LLM-as-Judge, KL divergence, and latency.
Reports some latency analysis and shows that the method can be implemented with modest overhead relative to controlled decoding in the tested setting.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: robust inference-time best-of-K and max-min/group-robust alignment have been explored in prior work (e.g., Yoon et al., 2024; MaxMin-RLHF; group-robust preference optimization). The paper's core idea is an incremental combination of controlled decoding with a minimax reweighting scheme, and the claim of being first to consider maxmin robust inference-time alignment is not adequately substantiated.

Theory-practice mismatch: the derived optimal policy samples from a softmax over weighted values, but Algorithm 1 selects the argmax block among K samples. This makes the practical algorithm a greedy robust best-of-K heuristic rather than the claimed Nash-equilibrium policy optimizer, and undermines the theoretical guarantees for the implemented method.

The weight update in Equation (10)/Algorithm 1 updates w multiplicatively without specifying a simplex projection or normalization. If w is constrained to the simplex, the update generally leaves the simplex unless followed by projection/normalization, which is not shown. The derivation treats logits, but the algorithm operates directly on w, creating ambiguity and a potential technical flaw.

Evaluation is not fully convincing. Several main comparisons are only against UNIFORM or individual-objective baselines, especially on UltraFeedback and ValuePrism. The LLM-as-Judge improvement over CD-UNIFORM is small (59.1% vs. 57.6%) and lacks statistical significance tests; no human evaluation is provided. The model scale is limited (gemma-2-2b-it) and relies on relatively small reward/value models.

The paper does not comprehensively report average reward trade-offs across all datasets and objectives. Since the method optimizes worst-case performance, it may sacrifice average quality; this is not systematically analyzed, and the main text often focuses on worst-case improvements.

Reproducibility is weakened by the blank/missing code link in the reproducibility statement despite saying code is available, and by incomplete details about simplex projection, reward normalization, value-function training, and some table entries (e.g., missing latency values for some methods).

The claims are stronger than the evidence in places: 'without any information about relative importance' ignores the need for lambda, K, block size, and reward scaling; 'minimal overhead' is only tested in one setting; and the positioning relative to prior robust best-of-K work is insufficiently clear.

strengths: Introduces a novel inference-time robust multi-objective decoding algorithm (RMOD) with a clear max-min game formulation and Nash equilibrium analysis.

Provides a solid theoretical derivation: the inner policy maximization has a closed-form best response, the weight minimization reduces to a convex log-sum-exp optimization, and KKT analysis explains weight sparsity and worst-case equalization.

The practical blockwise algorithm is well motivated, scalable, and achieves low latency compared with controlled decoding baselines; the distilled variant further reduces inference cost while preserving strong performance.

Experiments are extensive and cover three multi-objective alignment datasets (HH, UltraFeedback, ValuePrism), up to ten objectives, several baselines (CD variants, GRPO/DPO, MO-GRPO/MO-DPO, RS, MOD), and multiple evaluation angles (worst-case reward, win rate, LLM-as-judge, ablations on B/K/lambda, latency, qualitative examples).
The paper is generally reproducible: code is anonymized/open, models and datasets are public, and details are provided in the appendix.
Results consistently show improved worst-case alignment over baselines, and the method remains effective even when objectives are positively correlated or the number of objectives increases.
weaknesses: The notion of robustness is limited to worst-case weighting over known reward/value functions. Since min over the simplex of a weighted sum reduces to min_g V_g, the game formulation is mathematically somewhat overparameterized for the stated objective, and it does not address reward-model misspecification, distribution shift, or adversarial prompts.

The practical weight update in Algorithm 1/Equation 10 is not clearly projected onto the simplex. Multiplicative updates do not generally preserve the sum-to-one constraint, yet the theory assumes weights lie on the simplex. This gap between theory and implementation is not adequately addressed and could affect whether the algorithm truly solves the intended convex problem.

Theoretical guarantees rely on exact value functions and exact expectations, but the practical algorithm uses approximate value functions and K sampled blocks. There is no formal convergence or error analysis bounding the effect of these approximations.

Approximating the best-response policy by selecting the highest weighted-value candidate among K samples is coarse and no analysis is provided to show how close this is to the true optimal robust policy.

Empirical gains are sometimes modest: in the LLM-as-Judge evaluation, RMOD improves worst-case win rate over CD-UNIFORM by only about 1.5%, and statistical significance/confidence intervals are not reported. In several datasets, the same reward models are used for value training and evaluation, raising possible reward-overoptimization concerns.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior robust/group-robust best-of-K decoding work; the main new element is the controlled-decoding value-function version and its convex/max-min formulation. Some multi-objective baselines may not be fully tuned, and the paper does not fully rule out that baseline underperformance is due to implementation choices.

The method still requires several hyperparameters (lambda, block size B, number of candidates K, number of weight-update iterations I), so the claim of requiring no information about objective importance, while true in a narrow sense, does not make the method hyperparameter-free.
Some experimental details and tables are incomplete or unclear in the manuscript (e.g., Distill-RMOD latency and the exact simplex normalization/projection procedure).
